answer_text:
The degree of the product is

\[
19\cdot 3+8\cdot 2+6\cdot 4=57+16+24=97.
\]

For a monic polynomial

\[
F(x)=x^d+cx^{d-1}+\cdots,
\]

the coefficient of \(x^{de-1}\) in \(F(x)^e\) is \(ec\). Therefore, the coefficient of \(x^{96}\) in the product is

\[
19p+8q+6(-1)=19p+8q-6.
\]

We are told this coefficient is \(391\), so

\[
19p+8q-6=391
\]

\[
19p+8q=397.
\]

Modulo \(8\),

\[
19p\equiv 397 \pmod 8
\]

\[
3p\equiv 5 \pmod 8.
\]

Since \(3^{-1}\equiv 3\pmod 8\),

\[
p\equiv 15\equiv 7 \pmod 8.
\]

Thus all integer possibilities are

\[
p=8k+7,\qquad q=33-19k \qquad (k\in\mathbb Z).
\]

Every such pair gives integer coefficients throughout the product, so the \(a_i\) will automatically be integers.

As written, \(k\) can be arbitrarily negative, so \(p\) is unbounded below. For example, \(k=-1\) gives \(p=-1,\ q=52\), which works. Hence there is **no smallest integer value of \(p\)** under the literal statement.

If the intended condition was that \(p\) is nonnegative or positive, then the smallest value occurs at \(k=0\), giving

\[
p=7,\qquad q=33.
\]

So under that usual intended positivity assumption, the answer is

\[
\boxed{7}
\]
